hints: Look at each oxygen containing group carefully. Compare $\text{C(=O)OH}$ with $\text{C(=O)OR}$ and compare $\text{OH}$ attached directly to the benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ attached to other carbons.
Look at the nitrogen group in F. Check whether the $\text{NH}_2$ is joined directly to the benzene ring and recall the special name for that arrangement.
walkthrough:
Read F piece by piece**
In F you see a benzene ring with two substituents. One is $\text{NH}_2$ joined straight onto the ring. That is not just any amine, it is an aromatic amine, often called phenylamine. The other is $\text{C(=O)OH}$, which is the classic carboxylic acid group.

Read J piece by piece**
In J you also see a benzene ring with two substituents. One is $\text{OH}$ joined straight onto the ring, so that is a phenol, not an alcohol and not a carboxylic acid. The other is $\text{C(=O)O}$ joined to a saturated ring. A carbonyl joined to an $\text{O}$ joined to another carbon is the ester group.

Final answer: In F: (primary aromatic) amine / phenylamine and carboxylic acid.
In J: phenol and ester.

hints: Remember a chiral centre is a tetrahedral carbon with four different groups. Check for planar $sp^2$ carbons first, then look for carbons on the saturated ring with two identical methyl groups versus two different paths round the ring.
walkthrough:
Apply the four different groups test**
A chiral centre must be a saturated, tetrahedral carbon with four different attachments. All the carbons in F are either in the flat benzene ring or in the flat $\text{COOH}$ group, so none can be chiral. That gives 0 for F.
In J, the benzene part also gives nothing, so focus on the saturated six membered ring. The carbon joined to the ester oxygen and the carbon joined to the single $\text{CH}_3$ group each have four different groups. The carbon bearing two identical $\text{CH}_3$ groups cannot be chiral. That gives 2 for J.
Final answer: Number of chiral centres in F = 0 and in J = 2.

hints: Step 1 converts benzene to methylbenzene. Recall which halogenoalkane and which Lewis acid catalyst are used to attach an alkyl group to a benzene ring.
Step 2 nitrates methylbenzene. Think about whether the $\text{CH}_3$ group pushes electrons into the ring and which positions, 2,4,6 or 3,5, it activates, then match this to product E in step 3.
Step 4 converts $\text{NO}_2$ to $\text{NH}_2$ while leaving $\text{COOH}$ unchanged. Recall the specific metal plus concentrated acid combination for this selective reduction.
walkthrough:
Build the methylbenzene first**
Step 1 is electrophilic substitution of benzene by an alkyl group. The standard way is Friedel-Crafts alkylation using chloromethane, $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$, with the catalyst $\text{AlCl}_3$. That generates the $\text{CH}_3^+$ electrophile equivalent and gives methylbenzene.

Work out where nitration goes**
Step 2 is nitration with concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$ and concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$. The $\text{CH}_3$ group is electron donating and 2,4,6 directing. Step 3 then oxidises the $\text{CH}_3$ in D to $\text{COOH}$ to give 4-nitrobenzoic acid, E. So D must already have the $\text{NO}_2$ para to the $\text{CH}_3$. That is 4-nitrotoluene.

Reduce nitro without touching the acid**
Step 4 changes $\text{O}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-COOH}$ to $\text{H}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-COOH}$. This is reduction of an aromatic nitro group to a primary amine. Use hot tin, Sn, with concentrated $\text{HCl}$, followed by work up. This leaves the carboxylic acid intact.

Final answer: Step 1: $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$ and $\text{AlCl}_3$ (Friedel-Crafts alkylation).
D is 4-nitrotoluene, $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{NO}_2$ para to each other on benzene.
Step 4: hot Sn and concentrated $\text{HCl}$.

hints: Compare the order of steps. In Fig. 4.2 the $\text{CH}_3$ is oxidised to $\text{COOH}$ before nitration, so think about which substituent is directing the incoming $\text{NO}_2^+$ in this second route.
Recall whether $\text{COOH}$ donates or withdraws electrons and whether such groups direct to 2,4,6 or to 3,5 positions.
walkthrough:
Spot what controls the position now**
In the second route benzoic acid, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$, is nitrated directly. The group already on the ring is $\text{COOH}$, not $\text{CH}_3$, so it controls where $\text{NO}_2^+$ attacks.

Link withdrawing to meta direction**
$\text{COOH}$ pulls electrons away from the ring by the negative inductive and conjugative effect. It deactivates the ring and destabilises the intermediate for 2,4,6 attack more than for 3,5 attack. Nitration therefore goes mainly to the meta position, giving 3-nitrobenzoic acid as G, not the para isomer E.

Final answer: G is 3-nitrobenzoic acid, $\text{COOH}$ and $\text{NO}_2$ meta to each other on benzene.
$\text{COOH}$ is an electron withdrawing, deactivating, meta (3,5) directing group, so nitration occurs meta to $\text{COOH}$.

hints: J is an ester that splits into K, the acid part, plus L, the alcohol part. Focus on the saturated ring fragment that leaves with the oxygen and count its carbons, hydrogens and single oxygen.
walkthrough:
Isolate the alcohol fragment**
Alkaline hydrolysis of the ester followed by acidification gives the carboxylic acid K plus the alcohol L. L is the saturated $\text{C}_6$ ring plus one $\text{CH}_3$ substituent plus two $\text{CH}_3$ substituents on another carbon, plus the $\text{OH}$ formed from the ester oxygen. Counting gives 9 carbons, 18 hydrogens and 1 oxygen: $\text{C}_9\text{H}_{18}\text{O}$.

hints: Think about what $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ does to the $\text{COOR}$ linkage in J.
Think about what $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ also does to the $\text{OH}$ group attached directly to the benzene ring in J and in K.
walkthrough:
Break the ester**
The $\text{COO}$ linkage to the saturated ring is an ester. With $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ it undergoes alkaline hydrolysis to give a carboxylate salt plus the alcohol L.

Neutralise the phenol as well**
J also contains a phenolic $\text{OH}$ on the benzene ring. Phenols are acidic enough to react with $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ in an acid base or neutralisation reaction to give a phenoxide salt plus water. Acidification afterwards regenerates the phenol and the carboxylic acid.

Final answer: 1. hydrolysis (of ester)
2. acid-base / neutralisation (of phenol).

hints: Recall the general reaction of a compound containing an $\text{O-H}$ group with reactive metal sodium and what gas is released.
walkthrough:
Write the phenol to phenoxide change**
Phenol behaves as an acid toward Na metal. The $\text{O-H}$ proton is removed to give sodium phenoxide, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^{-}\text{Na}^{+}$, and hydrogen gas, $\text{H}_2$. Balance with $\tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_2$ for one mole of phenol.
Final answer: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{Na} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^{-}\text{Na}^{+} + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_2$

hints: Remember phenol is so activated that bromine water reacts without a catalyst and substitutes at all available 2,4,6 positions.
walkthrough:
Place three bromines around the phenol**
Excess $\text{Br}_2\text{(aq)}$ with phenol gives electrophilic substitution at the highly activated 2,4 and 6 positions. Draw phenol with $\text{OH}$ at the top and Br atoms ortho, ortho and para to it. That is 2,4,6-tribromophenol.
Final answer: N is 2,4,6-tribromophenol: benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ and Br at the 2,4,6 positions relative to $\text{OH}$.

hints: Compare which $\text{O-H}$ bond breaks more easily, the $\text{(CO)O-H}$ in the $\text{COOH}$ group of K or the phenolic $\text{O-H}$, and think about bond weakness and $\text{H}^{+}$ donation.
Think about how the nearby $\text{C=O}$ pulls electrons and how this affects the stability of the negative ion left after the proton is lost.
walkthrough:
Compare the O-H bonds**
Acidity means ease of losing $\text{H}^{+}$. In K the most acidic proton is on the carboxylic acid $\text{COOH}$, not the phenol group. That $\text{O-H}$ bond is more polarised and weaker because the adjacent $\text{C=O}$ pulls electrons away.

Compare the anions left behind**
Losing $\text{H}^{+}$ from $\text{COOH}$ gives a carboxylate ion where the negative charge is delocalised over two oxygens. This electron withdrawing stabilisation makes the anion much more stable than the phenoxide ion from phenol. A more stable conjugate base means a stronger acid, so K is stronger than phenol.

Final answer: The (CO)O-H bond in K is weaker / donates $\text{H}^{+}$ more easily owing to the negative inductive / electron withdrawing effect of C=O / $\text{COOH}$.
The carboxylate anion formed is stabilised (more than phenoxide), so K is a stronger acid than phenol.

hints: Think about what the lone pair on the phenolic oxygen can do with the pi system of the benzene ring.
Consider how that movement of electrons changes the electron density in the ring compared with plain benzene.
Link higher electron density in the ring to how strongly an electrophile such as $\text{NO}_2^+$ is attracted.
walkthrough:
See the lone pair joining the ring**
In phenol the oxygen has a p-orbital containing a lone pair that can overlap sideways with the pi system of the benzene ring. Picture that lone pair spreading or delocalising into the ring.

Build up electron richness**
Because of this donation, the benzene ring in phenol has higher electron density than benzene itself. It is activated.

Attract the electrophile more easily**
Nitration needs the ring to attract the $\text{NO}_2^+$ electrophile. A more electron rich ring attracts and polarises the electrophile much better, so phenol reacts with just dilute $\text{HNO}_3$, while benzene needs concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$ plus concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to generate a more powerful nitrating mixture.

Final answer: p-orbital on oxygen overlaps with ring pi system / lone pair on oxygen delocalised into ring.
Electron density in ring increases.
Electrophile attracted / polarised more easily, so milder nitration conditions work for phenol.
